newClaim.claimText: Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.
newClaim.claimValue: University of Toronto graduate students must clearly describe and cite any generative AI tools used in thesis research or writing.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Careful attention must be paid in the thesis to appropriately citing and describing any use of generative AI tools in the research process. It must be clear to the reader which generative AI tools were used, as well as how and why they were used.

SGS does not regulate master’s-level theses, Major Research Papers, or qualifying / comprehensive exams. However, SGS recommends that graduate units make use of the principles outlined for doctoral-level work in articulating requirements for any master’s-level research-based works.

newClaim.claimText: The University of Toronto does not support the use of AI-detection software on student work, because none has been found sufficiently reliable and sharing student work with such programs without permission raises privacy and ethical concerns. Instructors are encouraged to use traditional methods instead, such as meeting with the student to discuss their work.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: The University does not support the use of AI-detection software programs on student work. None of these software programs have been found to be sufficiently reliable, and they are known to incorrectly flag instances of AI use in human-written content.
In addition, sharing your students’ work (i.e., their intellectual property) with these software programs without their permission also raises a range of privacy and ethical concerns.

However, instructors are encouraged to continue to use their traditional methods for detection of potential academic misconduct, including meeting with a student to discuss their work in person, using short in-person assessments that ask students to expand on the ideas in their out-of-class assignments, and so on.

newClaim.claimText: The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

Normally such discussions are held synchronously, in person or virtually. Nothing the student says in such a discussion may be used or receivable in evidence against the student in the hearing of any charge with respect to the alleged offence in question.

newClaim.claimText: The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Undergraduate and graduate students may use GenAI tools as learning aids, for example, to summarize information or test their understanding of a topic. These tools should be used in a manner similar to consulting library books, online sources, peers, or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has stated that AI tools are not otherwise permitted in the course. These uses typically do not need to be cited or disclosed.

However, if students use information from GenAI tools that would normally require citation (e.g., quoting, paraphrasing, or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite their use according to guidelines provided by U of T Libraries or as directed by their instructor.

newClaim.claimText: University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Students must be able to opt out. You cannot require students to accept a third party’s terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property. If the tool is part of a required activity or assessment, you must provide a viable alternative for students who decline.

A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) is required wherever personally identifying information is collected. Under U of T’s FIPPA obligations, any unvetted tool that collects personal information (e.g., student names, email addresses, assessment submissions) needs a PIA to be conducted. This process typically takes four to eight weeks from the time all required information has been received.

newClaim.claimText: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.
newClaim.claimValue: ai_use_requires_instructor_permission

evidence.evidenceSnippet: to use or possess an unauthorized aid or aids or obtain or provide unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work;

if an instructor specified that no outside assistance was permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider a student’s use of generative AI to be use of an “unauthorized aid” under the Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters.
If your instructor advised you that use of AI tools was prohibited, using a generative AI tool to create even part of your marked assignment would be considered use of an unauthorized aid.

newClaim.claimText: University of Toronto teaching guidance (CTSI) now names Cogniti as the preferred tool for teaching and learning, embedded in Quercus and free for every student, and Microsoft Copilot Chat as the easiest general-purpose starting point available to everyone at U of T. Tools in the AI Kitchen are vetted and may be used with institutional data up to Level 3. Some licensed tools require a paid subscription not covered by the University. Tool availability does not authorize AI use in a given assessment.
newClaim.claimValue: microsoft_copilot_recommended_protected_tool_up_to_level_3_data

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Cogniti is the preferred tool for teaching and learning. It is built for education: embedded in Quercus, free for every student, highly customizable, and can be grounded in your course content.
Microsoft Copilot Chat is the easiest place to start. It is a general-purpose tool available to everyone at U of T and is the lowest-barrier way for students to build basic AI literacy.

Licensed Tools in the AI Kitchen (such as Claude for Education, ChatGPT Edu and M365 Copilot) may suit your own course preparation and other projects where advanced features can add value. However, some of these tools require a paid subscription that is not covered by the University.

Tools in the AI Kitchen are vetted for privacy and security and covered by U of T’s data protection standards: your prompts and your students’ data are never used to train AI models, and you can use institutional data up to Level 3, such as course materials and student assessments.

sourceChanges.citationTitle: Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (approved June 24, 2025; effective July 1, 2025)
Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom: FAQs (updated October 2026)
Using ChatGPT or other generative AI tool on a marked assessment (academic integrity scenario; cites pre-2025 Code numbering)
Welcome to the AI Kitchen (AI tools directory)
GenAI Tools for Teaching (CTSI)
Generative AI Tools (UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning)
Guidance on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (SGS, last updated September 9, 2026)
Use AI intelligently (Information Security guidelines)

claimChanges.claimText: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

The University of Toronto AI Kitchen lists ChatGPT Edu (OpenAI) for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing with limited seats, requested through the IT Service Centre. It is not listed as a student tool or as free.

University of Toronto teaching guidance (CTSI) now names Cogniti as the preferred tool for teaching and learning, embedded in Quercus and free for every student, and Microsoft Copilot Chat as the easiest general-purpose starting point available to everyone at U of T. Tools in the AI Kitchen are vetted and may be used with institutional data up to Level 3. Some licensed tools require a paid subscription not covered by the University. Tool availability does not authorize AI use in a given assessment.
The AI Kitchen Chef's Kit lists Microsoft Azure AI Foundry as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.
The AI Kitchen lists Claude for Education (Anthropic) for staff, faculty and librarians as free with limited seats, requested through the IT Service Centre. It is not listed as a student tool.

Contact North AI Tutor Pro is no longer listed in the central AI Kitchen directory, but the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning still lists Contact North AI tools as approved and publicly accessible (no UTORid required), describing AI Tutor Pro as supporting students' knowledge and skill building. This is a campus teaching-centre listing, not a central approval record, and it does not authorize use in a particular assessment.

Contact North AI Teacher's Assistant Pro is no longer listed in the central AI Kitchen directory, but the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it among approved, publicly accessible Contact North AI tools that help instructors create syllabi and resources. Removal from the central directory is not evidence that it is prohibited.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Copilot Chat for students, staff, faculty and librarians as Available and free, accessed by signing in with a U of T account.

The AI Kitchen lists M365 Copilot (integrated across Word, Excel, Teams and Outlook) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing through the IT Service Centre. It is a separate licence beyond the free Copilot Chat, and CTSI notes it is not centrally funded.

Scopus AI is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, integrated into the Scopus database. It is a library research-database feature, not a general assessment permission.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Teams Premium (AI meeting and lecture assistant) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.

Web of Science Research Assistant is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, built into the Web of Science database. It is a library research-database feature.

For graduate academic milestones generally (for example comprehensive exams, candidacy and other scholarly activities), the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies recommends that students seek and document in writing unambiguous approval from their supervisor(s) and supervisory committee before using generative AI. This general recommendation sits alongside stricter mandatory rules for the doctoral thesis (see claim-university-of-toronto-001); students, supervisors and graduate units must agree in advance how any AI tools will be used for each milestone.

The University of Toronto recommends that instructors include a syllabus statement informing students of their expectations on AI use, and provides sample statements for syllabi and assignments for graduate and undergraduate courses; some units may have their own guidelines. The earlier Vice-Provost URL now redirects to the office home page, so the current Vice-Provost, Teaching & Learning FAQ (updated October 2026) is used as the source.

University of Toronto Information Security guidelines state that no data should be provided to generative AI if any part of it should not appear in that system's results, and that before sharing personal information or university data classified as Level 2, 3 or 4 with any AI tool, users must verify the tool has been assessed by the university as suitable for that data type and level. AI Kitchen tools are approved for Level 3 data or below, except the Model Comparison Tool, which is approved only up to Level 2.

For the doctoral thesis specifically, the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies requires that the use of generative AI tools in any aspect of researching or writing the thesis be done with the prior approval of the supervisor(s) and supervisory committee. Students remain responsible for any AI-generated content in the thesis and must be able to describe and defend any AI use at the final oral examination.

Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.

The University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies states that unauthorized use of generative AI tools for scholarly work may be considered an offence under the Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters and research misconduct under the Policy on Ethical Conduct in Research and the Framework to Address Allegations of Research Misconduct. This is a possible consequence, not an automatic finding or sanction.

The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

Unless they have explicit permission from the instructor, University of Toronto students may not upload, copy, input or share course materials created or provided by the instructor, teaching assistants or the University (such as lecture slides, recordings, test questions, solutions and rubrics) to a generative AI tool that the University has not approved for that purpose. As a general rule students should not upload course materials into GenAI systems, because of model training and copyright concerns.

The University of Toronto does not support the use of AI-detection software on student work, because none has been found sufficiently reliable and sharing student work with such programs without permission raises privacy and ethical concerns. Instructors are encouraged to use traditional methods instead, such as meeting with the student to discuss their work.

The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

The AI Kitchen also lists Cogniti (course-specific AI virtual tutors grounded in instructor materials) for faculty, free with limited seats; students use Cogniti agents that instructors have enabled in Quercus courses, and instructors must request the ability to create agents. The Chef's Kit lists Microsoft GitHub Copilot Business for staff, faculty and librarians, free with limited seats.

The AI Kitchen lists three U of T-built services as Coming Soon (not yet available) for staff, faculty and librarians: the AIK Model Comparison Tool (approved only for data up to Level 2), the AIK Platform powered by Cohere, and AIK Dev.

The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Copilot Chat for students, staff, faculty and librarians as Available and free, accessed by signing in with a U of T account.

The AI Kitchen lists M365 Copilot (integrated across Word, Excel, Teams and Outlook) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing through the IT Service Centre. It is a separate licence beyond the free Copilot Chat, and CTSI notes it is not centrally funded.

Scopus AI is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, integrated into the Scopus database. It is a library research-database feature, not a general assessment permission.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Teams Premium (AI meeting and lecture assistant) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.

Web of Science Research Assistant is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, built into the Web of Science database. It is a library research-database feature.

For graduate academic milestones generally (for example comprehensive exams, candidacy and other scholarly activities), the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies recommends that students seek and document in writing unambiguous approval from their supervisor(s) and supervisory committee before using generative AI. This general recommendation sits alongside stricter mandatory rules for the doctoral thesis (see claim-university-of-toronto-001); students, supervisors and graduate units must agree in advance how any AI tools will be used for each milestone.

The University of Toronto recommends that instructors include a syllabus statement informing students of their expectations on AI use, and provides sample statements for syllabi and assignments for graduate and undergraduate courses; some units may have their own guidelines. The earlier Vice-Provost URL now redirects to the office home page, so the current Vice-Provost, Teaching & Learning FAQ (updated October 2026) is used as the source.

University of Toronto Information Security guidelines state that no data should be provided to generative AI if any part of it should not appear in that system's results, and that before sharing personal information or university data classified as Level 2, 3 or 4 with any AI tool, users must verify the tool has been assessed by the university as suitable for that data type and level. AI Kitchen tools are approved for Level 3 data or below, except the Model Comparison Tool, which is approved only up to Level 2.

For the doctoral thesis specifically, the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies requires that the use of generative AI tools in any aspect of researching or writing the thesis be done with the prior approval of the supervisor(s) and supervisory committee. Students remain responsible for any AI-generated content in the thesis and must be able to describe and defend any AI use at the final oral examination.

Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.

The University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies states that unauthorized use of generative AI tools for scholarly work may be considered an offence under the Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters and research misconduct under the Policy on Ethical Conduct in Research and the Framework to Address Allegations of Research Misconduct. This is a possible consequence, not an automatic finding or sanction.

The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

Unless they have explicit permission from the instructor, University of Toronto students may not upload, copy, input or share course materials created or provided by the instructor, teaching assistants or the University (such as lecture slides, recordings, test questions, solutions and rubrics) to a generative AI tool that the University has not approved for that purpose. As a general rule students should not upload course materials into GenAI systems, because of model training and copyright concerns.

The University of Toronto does not support the use of AI-detection software on student work, because none has been found sufficiently reliable and sharing student work with such programs without permission raises privacy and ethical concerns. Instructors are encouraged to use traditional methods instead, such as meeting with the student to discuss their work.

The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

The AI Kitchen also lists Cogniti (course-specific AI virtual tutors grounded in instructor materials) for faculty, free with limited seats; students use Cogniti agents that instructors have enabled in Quercus courses, and instructors must request the ability to create agents. The Chef's Kit lists Microsoft GitHub Copilot Business for staff, faculty and librarians, free with limited seats.

The AI Kitchen lists three U of T-built services as Coming Soon (not yet available) for staff, faculty and librarians: the AIK Model Comparison Tool (approved only for data up to Level 2), the AIK Platform powered by Cohere, and AIK Dev.

sourceChanges.citationTitle: Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (approved June 24, 2025; effective July 1, 2025)
Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom: FAQs (updated October 2026)
Using ChatGPT or other generative AI tool on a marked assessment (academic integrity scenario; cites pre-2025 Code numbering)
Welcome to the AI Kitchen (AI tools directory)
GenAI Tools for Teaching (CTSI)
Generative AI Tools (UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning)
Guidance on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (SGS, last updated September 9, 2026)
Use AI intelligently (Information Security guidelines)

claimChanges.claimText: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

The University of Toronto AI Kitchen lists ChatGPT Edu (OpenAI) for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing with limited seats, requested through the IT Service Centre. It is not listed as a student tool or as free.

University of Toronto teaching guidance (CTSI) now names Cogniti as the preferred tool for teaching and learning, embedded in Quercus and free for every student, and Microsoft Copilot Chat as the easiest general-purpose starting point available to everyone at U of T. Tools in the AI Kitchen are vetted and may be used with institutional data up to Level 3. Some licensed tools require a paid subscription not covered by the University. Tool availability does not authorize AI use in a given assessment.
The AI Kitchen Chef's Kit lists Microsoft Azure AI Foundry as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.
The AI Kitchen lists Claude for Education (Anthropic) for staff, faculty and librarians as free with limited seats, requested through the IT Service Centre. It is not listed as a student tool.

Contact North AI Tutor Pro is no longer listed in the central AI Kitchen directory, but the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning still lists Contact North AI tools as approved and publicly accessible (no UTORid required), describing AI Tutor Pro as supporting students' knowledge and skill building. This is a campus teaching-centre listing, not a central approval record, and it does not authorize use in a particular assessment.

Contact North AI Teacher's Assistant Pro is no longer listed in the central AI Kitchen directory, but the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it among approved, publicly accessible Contact North AI tools that help instructors create syllabi and resources. Removal from the central directory is not evidence that it is prohibited.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Copilot Chat for students, staff, faculty and librarians as Available and free, accessed by signing in with a U of T account.

The AI Kitchen lists M365 Copilot (integrated across Word, Excel, Teams and Outlook) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing through the IT Service Centre. It is a separate licence beyond the free Copilot Chat, and CTSI notes it is not centrally funded.

Scopus AI is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, integrated into the Scopus database. It is a library research-database feature, not a general assessment permission.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Teams Premium (AI meeting and lecture assistant) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.

Web of Science Research Assistant is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, built into the Web of Science database. It is a library research-database feature.

For graduate academic milestones generally (for example comprehensive exams, candidacy and other scholarly activities), the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies recommends that students seek and document in writing unambiguous approval from their supervisor(s) and supervisory committee before using generative AI. This general recommendation sits alongside stricter mandatory rules for the doctoral thesis (see claim-university-of-toronto-001); students, supervisors and graduate units must agree in advance how any AI tools will be used for each milestone.

The University of Toronto recommends that instructors include a syllabus statement informing students of their expectations on AI use, and provides sample statements for syllabi and assignments for graduate and undergraduate courses; some units may have their own guidelines. The earlier Vice-Provost URL now redirects to the office home page, so the current Vice-Provost, Teaching & Learning FAQ (updated October 2026) is used as the source.

University of Toronto Information Security guidelines state that no data should be provided to generative AI if any part of it should not appear in that system's results, and that before sharing personal information or university data classified as Level 2, 3 or 4 with any AI tool, users must verify the tool has been assessed by the university as suitable for that data type and level. AI Kitchen tools are approved for Level 3 data or below, except the Model Comparison Tool, which is approved only up to Level 2.

For the doctoral thesis specifically, the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies requires that the use of generative AI tools in any aspect of researching or writing the thesis be done with the prior approval of the supervisor(s) and supervisory committee. Students remain responsible for any AI-generated content in the thesis and must be able to describe and defend any AI use at the final oral examination.

Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.

The University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies states that unauthorized use of generative AI tools for scholarly work may be considered an offence under the Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters and research misconduct under the Policy on Ethical Conduct in Research and the Framework to Address Allegations of Research Misconduct. This is a possible consequence, not an automatic finding or sanction.

The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

Unless they have explicit permission from the instructor, University of Toronto students may not upload, copy, input or share course materials created or provided by the instructor, teaching assistants or the University (such as lecture slides, recordings, test questions, solutions and rubrics) to a generative AI tool that the University has not approved for that purpose. As a general rule students should not upload course materials into GenAI systems, because of model training and copyright concerns.

The University of Toronto does not support the use of AI-detection software on student work, because none has been found sufficiently reliable and sharing student work with such programs without permission raises privacy and ethical concerns. Instructors are encouraged to use traditional methods instead, such as meeting with the student to discuss their work.

The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

The AI Kitchen also lists Cogniti (course-specific AI virtual tutors grounded in instructor materials) for faculty, free with limited seats; students use Cogniti agents that instructors have enabled in Quercus courses, and instructors must request the ability to create agents. The Chef's Kit lists Microsoft GitHub Copilot Business for staff, faculty and librarians, free with limited seats.

The AI Kitchen lists three U of T-built services as Coming Soon (not yet available) for staff, faculty and librarians: the AIK Model Comparison Tool (approved only for data up to Level 2), the AIK Platform powered by Cohere, and AIK Dev.

sourceChanges.citationTitle: Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (approved June 24, 2025; effective July 1, 2025)
Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom: FAQs (updated October 2026)
Using ChatGPT or other generative AI tool on a marked assessment (academic integrity scenario; cites pre-2025 Code numbering)
Welcome to the AI Kitchen (AI tools directory)
GenAI Tools for Teaching (CTSI)
Generative AI Tools (UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning)
Guidance on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (SGS, last updated September 9, 2026)
Use AI intelligently (Information Security guidelines)

claimChanges.claimText: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

The University of Toronto AI Kitchen lists ChatGPT Edu (OpenAI) for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing with limited seats, requested through the IT Service Centre. It is not listed as a student tool or as free.

University of Toronto teaching guidance (CTSI) now names Cogniti as the preferred tool for teaching and learning, embedded in Quercus and free for every student, and Microsoft Copilot Chat as the easiest general-purpose starting point available to everyone at U of T. Tools in the AI Kitchen are vetted and may be used with institutional data up to Level 3. Some licensed tools require a paid subscription not covered by the University. Tool availability does not authorize AI use in a given assessment.
The AI Kitchen Chef's Kit lists Microsoft Azure AI Foundry as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.
The AI Kitchen lists Claude for Education (Anthropic) for staff, faculty and librarians as free with limited seats, requested through the IT Service Centre. It is not listed as a student tool.

Contact North AI Tutor Pro is no longer listed in the central AI Kitchen directory, but the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning still lists Contact North AI tools as approved and publicly accessible (no UTORid required), describing AI Tutor Pro as supporting students' knowledge and skill building. This is a campus teaching-centre listing, not a central approval record, and it does not authorize use in a particular assessment.

Contact North AI Teacher's Assistant Pro is no longer listed in the central AI Kitchen directory, but the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it among approved, publicly accessible Contact North AI tools that help instructors create syllabi and resources. Removal from the central directory is not evidence that it is prohibited.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Copilot Chat for students, staff, faculty and librarians as Available and free, accessed by signing in with a U of T account.

The AI Kitchen lists M365 Copilot (integrated across Word, Excel, Teams and Outlook) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing through the IT Service Centre. It is a separate licence beyond the free Copilot Chat, and CTSI notes it is not centrally funded.

Scopus AI is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, integrated into the Scopus database. It is a library research-database feature, not a general assessment permission.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Teams Premium (AI meeting and lecture assistant) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.

Web of Science Research Assistant is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, built into the Web of Science database. It is a library research-database feature.

For graduate academic milestones generally (for example comprehensive exams, candidacy and other scholarly activities), the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies recommends that students seek and document in writing unambiguous approval from their supervisor(s) and supervisory committee before using generative AI. This general recommendation sits alongside stricter mandatory rules for the doctoral thesis (see claim-university-of-toronto-001); students, supervisors and graduate units must agree in advance how any AI tools will be used for each milestone.

The University of Toronto recommends that instructors include a syllabus statement informing students of their expectations on AI use, and provides sample statements for syllabi and assignments for graduate and undergraduate courses; some units may have their own guidelines. The earlier Vice-Provost URL now redirects to the office home page, so the current Vice-Provost, Teaching & Learning FAQ (updated October 2026) is used as the source.

University of Toronto Information Security guidelines state that no data should be provided to generative AI if any part of it should not appear in that system's results, and that before sharing personal information or university data classified as Level 2, 3 or 4 with any AI tool, users must verify the tool has been assessed by the university as suitable for that data type and level. AI Kitchen tools are approved for Level 3 data or below, except the Model Comparison Tool, which is approved only up to Level 2.

For the doctoral thesis specifically, the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies requires that the use of generative AI tools in any aspect of researching or writing the thesis be done with the prior approval of the supervisor(s) and supervisory committee. Students remain responsible for any AI-generated content in the thesis and must be able to describe and defend any AI use at the final oral examination.

Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.

The University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies states that unauthorized use of generative AI tools for scholarly work may be considered an offence under the Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters and research misconduct under the Policy on Ethical Conduct in Research and the Framework to Address Allegations of Research Misconduct. This is a possible consequence, not an automatic finding or sanction.

The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

Unless they have explicit permission from the instructor, University of Toronto students may not upload, copy, input or share course materials created or provided by the instructor, teaching assistants or the University (such as lecture slides, recordings, test questions, solutions and rubrics) to a generative AI tool that the University has not approved for that purpose. As a general rule students should not upload course materials into GenAI systems, because of model training and copyright concerns.

The University of Toronto does not support the use of AI-detection software on student work, because none has been found sufficiently reliable and sharing student work with such programs without permission raises privacy and ethical concerns. Instructors are encouraged to use traditional methods instead, such as meeting with the student to discuss their work.

The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

The AI Kitchen also lists Cogniti (course-specific AI virtual tutors grounded in instructor materials) for faculty, free with limited seats; students use Cogniti agents that instructors have enabled in Quercus courses, and instructors must request the ability to create agents. The Chef's Kit lists Microsoft GitHub Copilot Business for staff, faculty and librarians, free with limited seats.

The AI Kitchen lists three U of T-built services as Coming Soon (not yet available) for staff, faculty and librarians: the AIK Model Comparison Tool (approved only for data up to Level 2), the AIK Platform powered by Cohere, and AIK Dev.

claimChanges.claimText: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

The University of Toronto AI Kitchen lists ChatGPT Edu (OpenAI) for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing with limited seats, requested through the IT Service Centre. It is not listed as a student tool or as free.

University of Toronto teaching guidance (CTSI) now names Cogniti as the preferred tool for teaching and learning, embedded in Quercus and free for every student, and Microsoft Copilot Chat as the easiest general-purpose starting point available to everyone at U of T. Tools in the AI Kitchen are vetted and may be used with institutional data up to Level 3. Some licensed tools require a paid subscription not covered by the University. Tool availability does not authorize AI use in a given assessment.
The AI Kitchen Chef's Kit lists Microsoft Azure AI Foundry as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.
The AI Kitchen lists Claude for Education (Anthropic) for staff, faculty and librarians as free with limited seats, requested through the IT Service Centre. It is not listed as a student tool.

Contact North AI Tutor Pro is no longer listed in the central AI Kitchen directory, but the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning still lists Contact North AI tools as approved and publicly accessible (no UTORid required), describing AI Tutor Pro as supporting students' knowledge and skill building. This is a campus teaching-centre listing, not a central approval record, and it does not authorize use in a particular assessment.

Contact North AI Teacher's Assistant Pro is no longer listed in the central AI Kitchen directory, but the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it among approved, publicly accessible Contact North AI tools that help instructors create syllabi and resources. Removal from the central directory is not evidence that it is prohibited.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Copilot Chat for students, staff, faculty and librarians as Available and free, accessed by signing in with a U of T account.

The AI Kitchen lists M365 Copilot (integrated across Word, Excel, Teams and Outlook) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing through the IT Service Centre. It is a separate licence beyond the free Copilot Chat, and CTSI notes it is not centrally funded.

Scopus AI is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, integrated into the Scopus database. It is a library research-database feature, not a general assessment permission.
The AI Kitchen lists Microsoft Teams Premium (AI meeting and lecture assistant) as Available for staff, faculty and librarians at negotiated pricing, requested through the IT Service Centre.

Web of Science Research Assistant is not in the central AI Kitchen directory; the UTSC Centre for Teaching and Learning lists it as an approved tool available in protected mode with UTORid login, built into the Web of Science database. It is a library research-database feature.

For graduate academic milestones generally (for example comprehensive exams, candidacy and other scholarly activities), the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies recommends that students seek and document in writing unambiguous approval from their supervisor(s) and supervisory committee before using generative AI. This general recommendation sits alongside stricter mandatory rules for the doctoral thesis (see claim-university-of-toronto-001); students, supervisors and graduate units must agree in advance how any AI tools will be used for each milestone.

The University of Toronto recommends that instructors include a syllabus statement informing students of their expectations on AI use, and provides sample statements for syllabi and assignments for graduate and undergraduate courses; some units may have their own guidelines. The earlier Vice-Provost URL now redirects to the office home page, so the current Vice-Provost, Teaching & Learning FAQ (updated October 2026) is used as the source.

University of Toronto Information Security guidelines state that no data should be provided to generative AI if any part of it should not appear in that system's results, and that before sharing personal information or university data classified as Level 2, 3 or 4 with any AI tool, users must verify the tool has been assessed by the university as suitable for that data type and level. AI Kitchen tools are approved for Level 3 data or below, except the Model Comparison Tool, which is approved only up to Level 2.

For the doctoral thesis specifically, the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies requires that the use of generative AI tools in any aspect of researching or writing the thesis be done with the prior approval of the supervisor(s) and supervisory committee. Students remain responsible for any AI-generated content in the thesis and must be able to describe and defend any AI use at the final oral examination.

Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.

The University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies states that unauthorized use of generative AI tools for scholarly work may be considered an offence under the Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters and research misconduct under the Policy on Ethical Conduct in Research and the Framework to Address Allegations of Research Misconduct. This is a possible consequence, not an automatic finding or sanction.

The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

Unless they have explicit permission from the instructor, University of Toronto students may not upload, copy, input or share course materials created or provided by the instructor, teaching assistants or the University (such as lecture slides, recordings, test questions, solutions and rubrics) to a generative AI tool that the University has not approved for that purpose. As a general rule students should not upload course materials into GenAI systems, because of model training and copyright concerns.

The University of Toronto does not support the use of AI-detection software on student work, because none has been found sufficiently reliable and sharing student work with such programs without permission raises privacy and ethical concerns. Instructors are encouraged to use traditional methods instead, such as meeting with the student to discuss their work.

The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

The AI Kitchen also lists Cogniti (course-specific AI virtual tutors grounded in instructor materials) for faculty, free with limited seats; students use Cogniti agents that instructors have enabled in Quercus courses, and instructors must request the ability to create agents. The Chef's Kit lists Microsoft GitHub Copilot Business for staff, faculty and librarians, free with limited seats.

The AI Kitchen lists three U of T-built services as Coming Soon (not yet available) for staff, faculty and librarians: the AIK Model Comparison Tool (approved only for data up to Level 2), the AIK Platform powered by Cohere, and AIK Dev.
